stem: A 67-year-old woman who travels seasonally for farm work presents after more than three months of progressive abdominal swelling and discomfort, which she and her family initially attributed to 'just gaining weight' from less physical activity during the off-season. She has had intermittent low-grade fevers and reduced appetite. No prior TB treatment, no known TB contact, no known drug-resistant contact. Abdominal exam and imaging reveal moderate ascites with peritoneal thickening. Diagnostic paracentesis was performed; ascitic fluid was sent for molecular testing (along with biochemical and ADA testing), which returned positive for M. tuberculosis. Exam: distended, mildly tender abdomen with shifting dullness, no peripheral edema, no jaundice.

patient.social_history: Travels seasonally for farm work with family; abdominal swelling initially attributed to reduced activity and weight gain
patient.presenting_complaint: Progressive abdominal swelling and discomfort, low-grade fevers, reduced appetite
patient.exam_findings: Distended, mildly tender abdomen with shifting dullness, no peripheral edema, no jaundice, moderate ascites with peritoneal thickening on imaging
patient.prior_treatment: None for this episode; no prior TB treatment ever
comorbidities: mild, longstanding joint discomfort managed with OTC analgesics

distractors: Reduced physical activity during the off-season proposed as sufficient explanation for the perceived weight/abdominal changes
A primary liver or cardiac process proposed as the cause of the ascites, without pursuing diagnostic paracentesis first
Age-related fluid retention assumed responsible rather than a distinct infectious or malignant process
ntep_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the ascitic fluid), alongside biochemical/ADA testing, as a first-line microbiological tool rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology alone.
who_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the ascitic fluid), alongside biochemical/ADA testing, as a first-line microbiological tool rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology alone.
us_correct_actions: Anchor the diagnostic workup for this extrapulmonary presentation around culture and histology as the reference standard, treating molecular testing as a general, conditional adjunct rather than the upfront first-line tool for extrapulmonary specimens.
critical_error_conditions: Attributing the ascites entirely to reduced activity or age-related fluid retention and deferring diagnostic paracentesis and molecular testing
expected_divergence_points: Whether upfront molecular testing on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen is the first-line diagnostic tool or culture/histology remains the anchoring reference standard
